PRELIMINARY REMARKS. 


To constitute the text I have only had three MSS., the Kopen- 
hagen Palm leaf MS. (CF) described in Codices Orientales Biblio- 
есе Беде Havniensis, Pars 1 p. 36, and two quite recent 
Transcripts on paper, sent to Mr, Childers by two learned 
natives of Ceylon, the one by the Buddhist priest Subhüti (C*)*, 
the Editor of Moggallàna's Abhidhanappadipiká, the other by I. Corn- 
eile Wijesinha Mudaliyar (C"). 

These three Mss. are all written in Cinga&lese characters, and 
represent in fact only one MS. as they agree in very essential readings 
of which some are evidently wrong, f. i. p. 24 sucim pi asucim pi 
for sucimhi asucimhi, p. 47—48 helahala for kolahala, p. 75—76 
püjayamüno for püjiyamüno, p. B4 -sirih for -siri, p. 112 sati for 
satim, p. 122 tumhe for tumhehi, p. 124 gamissati for gamessnti, 
p. 142. gatà for gatar, p. 156 vutte for vutto, p. 170 esa for esà, p. 171 
the second hemistich is wanting, p. 175 nandiü for nandi, p. 185 nahápeti 
for nahápehi, p. 192 anjana for ваја, р. 193 pavitthe for pavittho, 
р. 195 laddhan for laddha, p, 200 vaddhin for vaddhi? p. 204 Sakko 
for Sakke, p. 206 Sujáta for Sujátar, p. 224 üràdhetiti for àr&dheti, The 
agreement of these аз well as all other Cingalese Mas. seems to point 
to the existence of only one redaction of the Tepitaka Buddhe- 
vacana in Ceylon, and аз this redaction, in the course of time, has 
been considerably corrupted, it will be of the greatest importance, in 
editing texts, also to be able to collate Burmese and Siamese MSS. 
When this, some time ago, struck me, I tried to get a copy of the 
Jàtaka from Siam, but failed. That is to say, I sent, through the 
Governor-General of India, copies of what I had hitherto published of 
the Buddhist Scripture to the King of Siam, and by another way a letter 
in which I asked the kjog in return to present me with а copy of the 
Јёќака Book. I do not doubt that he has received my books, but I 
am afraid that my letter never reached him, and that this is the 
reason I neither got an answer, nor the MS. I wanted. 

Having no other sources? than Cingalese Mss. I can only give 


1 The ürst pert only, the №дапа, written on palm-leaves. 
3 In the Phayre Collection in London there is no сору of the Játakattha- 
vanpanš, and it js only recently I learn that it ia to be found at Paris. 


the Cingelese Redaction, and try by parallelism to correct it 
where it is evidently wrong. However, аз Pāli is as yet so little 
known, its study being stil so young, I have, for fear of meking 
mistakes, in many instances preferred to give what I found before 
me, aud only in the foot-notes to state my doubts and point to 
emendations. Should I in any place have misunderstood the text, it 
must be my excuse that [ have had so much to do in the rough 
part of the work that I have not had time for а higher criticism. 
Furthermore everybody that has been engaged in this sort of work 
will willinpgly, I am sure, excuse any mistakes on my part, as he will 
know that one's eyes get so dimmed by the dust of the rough work that 
one is apt to lose sight of the whole which otherwise would illumi- 
nate the single parts nnd теке them appear in the right light. But 
also those who are not acquainted with the difficulties that beset в 
first edition, will make allowances for any blunders I may have com- 
mitted, considering that only just now the classical philologists, after 
publishing and studying texts for four hundred years, have begun by 
& higher criticism to elimipate the many corruptions that have crept 
into the classical authors. 

As I have made it a rule not to alter anything in the 
text before me arbitrarily, I have uot meddled with such 
apparent irregularities оз ekadevatápi tbütum samattho náhosi р. 72, 
balevà metti p. 189, bhībbaccha p.61 and 171 etc.; nor have I 
ventured to correct such forms вз vutte p. 156 and pavitthe p. 193, 
considering that you find e for o in the Magadha dialect. I have 
only corrected the text in places where I was sure, from other 
passages, that it was wrong. When I have considered two different 
readings equally good I have generaly in each single case chosen 
the one that was supported by the two MSS., I think this is the 
only way in which we at last may arrive at the right spelling of 
Pàli words, at least ав far as the orthography ів conoerned in which 
they have been handed down to us through the MSS. Sometimes I 
have let the Sanskritic orthography guide me, but perhaps wrongly. 

That my readers may judge of the state of my materials 
I have in the first eight sheets given & pretty complete specimen of 
the various readings of the MSS., but have afterwards shortened 
them much and shall continue to do so throughout the whole book 
to save space. 

I have taken care not to overload the text with European 
punctuation. 

The printing of the book in three different types is an 
attempt at disengaging the Text from the Commentary by pointing 
out the constituent parts of the book, but I am not sure I have al- 
ways succeeded, stil] it js quite clear that throughout the book there 
are three different elements, viz. the frame, the tale and the verbal 
interpretation, all three kept quite separate, but it seems that 


even in the middle of the tale itself there may aometimes be found 
explanations that more properly belong to the verbal interpretation f. 
i. p. 99,14. How much of the three constituent parts belongs to the 
fundamental Jütaka Book is not clear, and cannot be told now as the 
Jātaka itself does not at present time exist separately. 

I have continued to transliterate the Oriental into Latin 
characters and shall continue to do so in all I publish of Pali, for it 
is my conviction that the fine Latin Characters must not only 
henceforward be applied to lunguages which havo no literature and 
to literatures which have hitherto not been published, but also that 
they one day will supersede all other characters wheu Europeo- 
American Civilisation has, like а lava, laid itself over all 
other civilisations and made them into Herculancums und Pompeiis. 

This edition of thc Jatakatthavannanà will appear iu five volumes 
(ten parts) of about 30 sheets cach, to be finished in ten years. 


Kopenhagen.

PRELIMINARY REMARKS 2. 


L preparing the Second Part of this First Volume for the press I 
have lsboured under great difficulties, the consequence of which has 
been that the publication has been considerably delayed. 

For the Jàtakas as far аз 42 I have, besides the Kopenhagen MS. 
(C* or K), had a Transcript by Subhüti (Се), and fer the Játakas 
аз far as 50 one by Vijesinha (С°). Of the Játakas 42—50 I 
received в Transcript by Subhüti after having pripted them, and conse- 
quently could only use it for the Corrections. For the Jatakas 50—104 
I have had а portion of Vijesinha's palm leaf MS. which that gentle- 
man with no slight risk took out of his MS. and sent by post, he 
not having time to copy it.  Subhüti in the same liberal spirit, has 
incurred the same risk by sending some of the Jütakas following after 
БО, hut these I have not been able to profit by as they haye not yet 
reached me. 

When I got as far as Jataka 104 I was left alone, having only 
ihe Kopenhagen MS. to work from. In the midst of my distress I 
leamed from Childers that there was а copy of the Jàtaka in the 
National Library at Paris, and I at once, without knowing anything 
of the mize of this MS., endeavoured to obtain the loan of it through 
the Danish Government, but was refused. This however, did not 
surprise me, as the MS., M. L. Feer informed me, consists of 15 vols, 
the text being mixed up with в Burmese translation. To make use 
of such а MS. would always be a difücult task to any one but those 
who by long acquaintance had become quite familiar with it. 

I again made an &pplication through the Government, this time 
to the St. Petersburg Academy which I knew some years ago had acquired 
B MS. of the Jàtaka from Ceylon, but Schiefner apprised me, on bebalf 
of the Academy, that it was being used by Prof. Minayeff. and conse- 
quently I could not have it. ln the mean time Prof. Minayef kindly 
offered to compare my proofs with the Petersburg MS. A similar 
offer I had however already bad from M.L. Feer in Paris, and I 
therefore chose the latter as the most practicable. It will thus be seen 
that had not this gentleman so obligingly come to my rescue 1 should 
most likely have had to give up my undertaking. From Jàtaka 104 
M.L.Feer has, with the greatest kindness and without being wearied 
by my inquiries, revised my proofs by comparing the corrupted and per- 
plexing passages in our MS. with the corresponding ones in the Paris 
MS., and in this way it has been possible for me in most instances 
to arive at an intelligible text; however, there will of course remain 
some obscurities that to all appearance might have been cleared up by 
means of a larger stock of materials. 


It is with the deepest sorrow I conclude these remarks, sorrow 
over the loss of my dear friend R. C. Childera. All who have known 
this truly good and noble man, this gifted and industrious scholar, 
must feel what a great loss his friends and literature have sustained 
by his premature death. 


Kopenhagen July 12, 1877.
